Comparing the street bearing to the face azimuths (southeast ~118.9, southwest ~209, northwest ~298.9, northeast ~29), I'm reasoning that the wall actually fronting the street should have its outward normal perpendicular to the street's direction, putting the facing wall's azimuth closer to 209.1 rather than the near-matching 118.9 value. Looking across floors on this north-west face, solar delta-T rises with height while the trap and sky components stay relatively flat, with the sky term showing a consistent net heat loss.

This confirms the panel is solar-dominated rather than trap-dominated—the wall's elevated temperature comes from absorbed shortwave radiation hitting the exterior surface, not conducted interior heat or reflected longwave from adjacent buildings. That distinction matters because insulation addresses conduction, not the solar absorption that's actually driving this wall's heat buildup.

That said, the key issue is attribution: the fix has to match the actual dominant driver, not just any plausible measure. Since this facade is heavily glazed (WWR roughly 0.5-0.75), solar gain through the glass is almost certainly the dominant pathway, not conduction through the opaque spandrel — so insulating the spandrel wouldn't address the real problem even if it seems intuitively related to "the wall getting hot."

I've identified the north-west face (azimuth 298.9°) as the worst-performing panel, running parallel to East 38th Street, peaking at 59.1°C in August. Every floor's schedule shows this face as solar-dominant, with dt_solar around 5-6K versus dt_trap near 0.8-0.9K, confirming it's heavily solar-driven rather than longwave-driven.

The wall_insulation measure applies only to floors 1-4, where attribution is 44% solar/56% longwave trap - a genuinely trap-dominated zone at the base where insulation logic makes sense. But the effect is counter-intuitive: d_facade_peak_k comes out positive at +0.567, meaning insulating the wall actually makes the surface HOTTER by roughly 0.57-1.05K in summer, not cooler as expected, applying to all ambient-facing walls at that band, not just the north-west face.

I'm trying to reconcile this - it seems like insulation reduces the heat that used to conduct away into the building, so it stays trapped at the surface instead, running the exterior hotter while keeping the interior cooler. But then I notice the annual kWh figures are also positive (4625.9 to 12322.5), which seems backwards for an insulation measure that should reduce cooling energy - unless these are framed as cost/savings context rather than raw usage, since the money figures also show positive dollar amounts for energy use and savings.

I'm untangling this seeming contradiction: wall insulation makes the exterior surface hotter in summer because heat that used to conduct into the cooler interior now stays trapped at the surface. But that same reduced conduction pathway should actually mean less heat reaching occupants inside, since the free-running interior model assumes no mechanical cooling — so the surface-temperature effect and the occupant-comfort effect may be telling different parts of the story rather than truly contradicting each other.

That's the smoking gun then: the wall gets warmer, not cooler, and person-hours of exposure go up by 3113, because insulating the exterior traps longwave radiation reflected from neighboring buildings right at the surface instead of letting it conduct away into the mass. The insulation layer blocks that conduction path, so the absorbed energy stays concentrated at the outer surface rather than dissipating inward.

But this measure only applies to the base floors 1-4 across all faces, not selectively to the East 38th Street wall on upper floors — the measure actually treating that upper-floor face is the glazing retrofit applied to floors 5-35.

Wall insulation isn't triggered for the upper floors because that facade is glazing-dominated (WWR 0.75), so the opaque wall area is minor there and glazing retrofit is the applicable fix instead. And even at floors 1-4 where wall insulation does apply, the physics shows it actually warms rather than cools the wall, since the base's heat balance is dominated by trapped longwave radiation (56%) over solar gain (44%).

Exactly this same pattern applies floor-by-floor: since 75% of the elevation is glazing with SHGC 0.5-0.8, and solar temperature swings (~5-6K) dwarf conduction swings (~0.8-0.9K), fabric insulation is essentially irrelevant compared to a glazing fix. I'm now tallying the affected area for this glazing retrofit across floors 5-35 on the north-west face, coming to roughly 6,122.5 m².

The peak reduction is modest at -0.727 K but seems repeated across prescriptions, suggesting it's a canyon-level average rather than measure-specific -- the seasonal breakdown is more telling, showing much stronger summer effects (-1.337 K facade, -0.565 K MRT) versus negligible winter impact, plus a small seasonal penalty of 0.547 K. Annual energy savings range from about 34,000 to 96,500 kWh/yr, peak demand drops by 54-133 kW, and there's a modest labor cost of 30 person-hours.

Financially the numbers look rough: energy and demand savings are only a few thousand to twenty-some thousand dollars per year, but capex runs $3-10 million with payback stretching from 63 to nearly 860 years, and NPV is deeply negative across the board (-$1.9M to -$10.3M) -- I need to flag this as a bad investment case, especially since half the underlying constants (capex per m², discount rate, electricity price, LL97 coefficient, measure life) are unverified. Since the glazing covers 75% of the elevation and shortwave solar gain accounts for roughly 69-80% of the positive heat drivers on the upper floors, an opaque-wall fix would leave most of the heat pathway untouched. Even where insulation is correctly targeted, the recalculated result is counter-intuitive: peak facade temperature rises rather than falls, since insulating the exterior traps absorbed longwave right at the surface instead of letting it conduct into the building mass and dissipate. text:
Insulating the opaque wall won't touch what's actually cooking those upper floors: on this face the heat is arriving as sun through glass, not as heat conducted through masonry, so a fabric measure treats a wall that is three-quarters window.

## Where the heat on that wall actually comes from

[560 Third Avenue](hc:building/1019099) sits at the corner of Third Avenue and East 38th Street, and its facade to the street runs along its north-west face. That face is confirmed against the street segment itself (canyon "E 38 ST", modelled sky view factor 0.36) rather than assumed from the address, and it carries the building's single worst point: a panel at the fifth floor peaking at 59.1 °C in August, 3,883 kelvin-hours a year above 35 °C (all MODELLED, surface temperature, not air).

The model splits every degree of that excess into what put it there: absorbed sun, longwave trapped from the buildings opposite, and relief radiated to the open sky. On this wall, floor by floor:

| Floor band | Absorbed shortwave | Longwave trapped | Dominant driver |
|---:|---:|---:|---|
| Ground (1–4, all faces) | 44% | 56% | trap |
| 5 (band 1) | 69% | 31% | solar |
| 22–35 (bands 6–9) | 77–80% | 20–23% | solar |

That flip is the finding: at street level the wall is genuinely heated by the buildings across the street reflecting and re-radiating at it, which is a legitimate case for fabric. But climb past the fourth floor and the building rises clear of its neighbours (the surrounding canyon averages only 14 m), and from there up the excess heat on this wall is overwhelmingly sun striking the surface directly, not trapped radiation. Per storey on the upper floors the solar term alone (5.1 to 5.9 K) runs five to six times the trapping term (0.8 to 0.9 K), on every one of floors 25 through 35 the model checked (MODELLED).

And on this wall the glass, not the masonry, is doing the absorbing: window-to-wall ratio here is 0.5 to 0.75 (ASSUMED, from the 1960s-70s curtain-wall era this tower belongs to, since no glazing survey exists for it). Insulating a spandrel that is at most a quarter of the elevation leaves three-quarters of the heat pathway completely untouched.

## What the physics actually selects, and what that costs

Wall insulation never triggered for this face above the fourth floor. What the model re-solves for it instead is a glazing retrofit to a low solar-heat-gain unit (target SHGC 0.25), because no shading device can be hung there either: at the 18:00 peak the sun is only 26° above the horizon and nearly square-on to the wall, so a fixed overhang would need to project 4.1 m against a 1.5 m limit, and vertical fins would need a depth three times their spacing. Both fail for the same reason and no larger version fixes it — the devices that work are either retractable, or the glass itself.

That retrofit, re-solved across floors 5–35 (6,123 m² of glazing):

- Cuts the summer facade peak by 1.3 K and the felt radiant temperature by 0.6 K, with almost no winter penalty (−0.01 K) — MODELLED.
- Removes an estimated 30,900 person-hours of exposure a year across the treated floors.
- Costs, on assumed 2023-vintage pricing that is mostly unverified, $3.06 million to $10.4 million in capital, against energy and demand savings of $12,100 to $48,200 a year — a payback of 63 to 860 years, and a negative net present value everywhere in that range. This is not a measure that pays for itself; it is a comfort and Local Law 97 compliance measure, and it should be priced and pitched as one, not as an energy retrofit.

The one place wall insulation *was* selected by the model, floors 1–4 (base of the tower, all four faces), is exactly where trapping dominates, and it is the most useful finding here: re-solved, it makes the wall's own peak surface temperature go **up**, by 0.6 K (0.57 to 1.05 K in summer), and increases person-hours of exposure by about 3,100 a year rather than cutting them. The mechanism is not subtle once you see it: this wall used to bleed the trapped radiation it absorbed into the cooler building mass behind it; insulate it and that heat has nowhere to go but stay at the outer skin, which then runs hotter. What it does save is winter heating, $1,350 to $5,345 a year against $270,000 to $1.08 million installed, a 50 to 800-year payback on energy alone. A cheaper and more effective lever for that same base problem exists in the model but isn't yours to build: raising the albedo of the facade across the street cuts 1.9 K off this same base wall for $72,000 to $324,000, because it treats the actual source of the trapped radiation rather than this building's response to it — worth raising with the block association or through NYC Accelerator's coordination pathway, not with your own contractor.

> The economics constants behind every dollar above are 2023-vintage and mostly unverified (24 of 33 constants in the table, including the glazing and insulation capex figures used here); treat the ranges as the honest spread of an era rule, not a quote, and get a real bid before committing capital.

So: tell the contractor to reprice this as a glazing job, not an insulation job, for the fifth floor and up, and to expect a bill in the millions with no energy payback inside the measure's working life — the case for doing it is comfort and code, not utility savings. For the ground floors, insulation is aimed at the right mechanism but delivers the wrong result in summer; if the goal there is relief from heat, that's a cooling-centre and assistance-referral problem this season, not a capital one.
